scenes.narration: Meet Anu. Today at school, Teacher Meena shares the Body Safety Rule: 'Your body belongs to YOU and no one else. Safe touches feel good and happy, like a high-five from a friend or a hug you asked for. If any touch makes you feel scared, funny, or mixed-up inside, you are allowed to say NO, loud and clear.' Anu wonders: what does this rule really mean?

choices.text: My body belongs to me, so I can say NO to any touch that feels wrong, even to a grown-up.
choices.feedback: Yes! That is exactly right. There is a special law in India that protects every child's body. You never have to be polite about a touch that feels wrong. Saying NO is always allowed, even to a grown-up.

choices.text: I have to let bigger people do whatever they say.
choices.feedback: No, and this is very important: no one, however big, is allowed to touch you in a way that feels wrong. Your body belongs to YOU, and the law protects that. You can always say NO.

scenes.narration: Teacher Meena tells a story. A child in the story gets a touch that feels mixed-up and wrong inside. Then the person whispers: 'This is our little secret. Do not tell anyone.' The child's tummy feels tight and worried. Teacher Meena asks the class: what should the child in the story do?

choices.text: Tell the secret to a trusted grown-up, like a parent or a teacher.
choices.feedback: Yes! A secret that makes you feel bad or worried inside is a secret you should ALWAYS tell. Telling is not tattling. It is brave, and it keeps children safe.

choices.text: Keep the secret, because the child promised.
choices.feedback: No promise can make a bad secret okay. Secrets about touching must always be told to a trusted grown-up. The child will NOT be in trouble for telling. Not ever.
Pretending does not make the worried feeling go away. The safe thing is to tell a trusted grown-up, who can make the bad thing stop.

scenes.narration: The child in the story decides to tell. But tell WHO? Teacher Meena asks: who counts as a trusted grown-up?

choices.text: Someone the child knows well and feels safe with, like Amma, Papa, or a teacher.
choices.feedback: Perfect. A trusted grown-up is someone you know well and feel safe with. And here is a superpower to remember: if a child ever cannot find one, there is a free phone friend called Childline. Just dial 1098, any day, any time.
People online can pretend to be anyone. For help, always go to a grown-up you know in real life, or call Childline on 1098. It is a free helpline just for children, open day and night.

scenes.narration: In the story, the child tells Amma everything. Amma gives a big, wanted hug and says: 'Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong. It is NEVER a child's fault. I will keep you safe now.' The child feels light and happy again. The whole class smiles. What did we learn?

choices.text: The child was brave to tell, and it was never the child's fault.
choices.feedback: Exactly right. When something wrong happens to a child, the fault belongs to the person who did it. NEVER the child. Telling a trusted grown-up, or calling Childline 1098, is always the right thing to do.

choices.text: The child should have kept the secret.
choices.feedback: No. Telling was exactly right. Bad secrets must always be told. The child did nothing wrong, and neither would you. Grown-ups who love you, and helpers like Childline 1098, are there to keep you safe.

quizQuestions.question: Who does your body belong to?
quizQuestions.explanation: Your body belongs to YOU. A special law in India called POCSO protects every child's body from wrong touch.

quizQuestions.question: A secret makes you feel scared or mixed-up inside. What should you do?
options: Tell a trusted grown-up, like a parent or teacher
quizQuestions.explanation: Bad secrets must always be told. A trusted grown-up can help, and Childline 1098 is a free phone friend for any child, any time.

quizQuestions.question: If someone touches a child in a wrong way, whose fault is it?
options: The person who did it. NEVER the child.
quizQuestions.explanation: It is NEVER the child's fault. The law is on the child's side, always, and telling a trusted grown-up is always right.
